title: Two Spirits
premise: A man dresses as a ghost to frighten his wife in a graveyard.
plays_out: A real shrouded skeleton appears beside him; he flees, but the women lock him out and he collapses unconscious until morning.
author: Traditional; specific published version listed in provenance
version_provenance: Johannes Wilhelm Wolf, Deutsche Märchen und Sagen (1845), no. 136, pp. 241–42; oral source.

title: The Death Shroud
premise: A servant steals a wandering dead man's shroud and hides inside a church.
plays_out: The corpse persuades him to pass a corner through the keyhole and bursts the door open; the servant is found nearly dead and dies young afterward.
author: Traditional; specific published version listed in provenance
version_provenance: Karl Eduard Haase, Volkstümliches aus der Grafschaft Ruppin und Umgegend, vol. 1 (1887), no. 49, p. 53; communicated by Teacher Fehse.

title: The Preacher and the Ghost
premise: A wife sends a sheet-covered servant to frighten her husband returning from midnight prayers.
plays_out: When the preacher challenges him, the servant starts sinking into the earth; his pleas cannot save him, and he disappears completely beneath it.
author: Traditional; specific published version listed in provenance
version_provenance: Arvid August Afzelius, Volkssagen und Volkslieder aus Schwedens älterer und neuerer Zeit, vol. 3 (1842), p. 245.

title: White Cap
premise: A girl mistakes a graveyard ghost for a familiar prankster and steals its cap.
plays_out: Ordered to replace it silently, she instead speaks; the ghost strikes her dead and sinks back into its grave.
author: Traditional; specific published version listed in provenance
version_provenance: Jón Arnason, Icelandic Legends, translated by George E. J. Powell and Eiríkur Magnússon (1864), pp. 157–58.

title: The Stolen Liver
premise: A husband spends the food money drinking, then substitutes a hanged man's liver for his wife's supper.
plays_out: The dead man arrives demanding it; when she questions him about his missing liver, he seizes and strangles her.
author: Traditional; specific published version listed in provenance
version_provenance: Otto Knoop, Ostmärkische Sagen, Märchen und Erzählungen (1909), no. 85, pp. 181–82.
